steps.title: How people actually change each other’s minds
steps.html:
The three moves. Almost every productive turn in a discussion has the same shape: concede something, object to the rest, propose what should happen instead. Well, you have got a point about the cost, but the timing is what worries me — could we start in April? Drop the concession and you sound like an opponent; drop the proposal and the discussion has nowhere to go.

Conceding is not losing. You have got a point, that is fair, I am all for that, I take your point all buy you the right to the word but. In English this is close to obligatory: an objection with no concession in front of it reads as hostility even when it is not meant that way.

Marking an opinion. As I see it, it seems to me that, personally, I think, I would say that all say the same thing: this is my reading, not a fact. It sounds weaker and it is strategically stronger, because you can move later without having to admit you were wrong.

Balancing. On the other hand and that said put a second consideration beside the first rather than knocking the first down. Use them when you want to complicate the picture, not win.

Closing a part. OK, I can agree with X. What about Y? is what turns a discussion into a decision. Say what is settled out loud, then name the next open question.

Question tags. …, do you not? and …, is it not? hand the turn back and invite agreement. In speech they are usually contracted: don’t you?, isn’t it?

steps.title: The commonest errors at this level
steps.html:
• Objecting with no concession: No. The cost is fine.
  • Stating opinions as facts: It is obvious that… in every turn.
  • Agreeing so completely that nothing is decided.
  • I am agree instead of I agree, and I am agree with you.
  • Using on the contrary where English wants on the other hand.

steps.title: Напиши свой текст
steps.sub: Напиши ответ, затем сверься с образцом
steps.modelHtml:
The discussion turned on which five qualities matter most in a teacher. The first speaker began with patience and kindness, arguing that learning is harder than it looks from the front of a room. The second accepted this but objected that a kind teacher who has no ideas teaches nothing, and pushed for creativity.

Two disagreements followed. The first speaker warned that a lesson can be enjoyable and empty; the second replied that a teacher can also be too nice, and proposed strictness. That was the only point neither would concede: strictness was called old-fashioned, and answered with the claim that motivated students do not waste time.

Four qualities were agreed — motivating, supportive, creative and hard-working — with organisation proposed as the fifth. The list was left one place short.
